titleStmt.title: EDF Schedulability Test for the E-TDL Time-Triggered Framework

analytic.title: EDF Schedulability Test for the E-TDL Time-Triggered Framework

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Time-triggered architectures bring to the applications a considerable degree of determinism and a strong conformity between their execution and their logical model. The Extended Timing Definition Language (E-TDL) is a timetriggered framework for programming real-time applications that can be structured through multiple independent components with fully adaptive behaviors. In this paper, we propose a schedulability test for E-TDL applications executed under Earliest Deadline First on a single processor. We derive an efficient solution for evaluating the maximal processor demand over the time intervals during which application may change its operational modes. We provide a detailed insight into the schedulability test procedure and discuss its complexity. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the current implementation of the test.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The use of the time-triggered paradigm helps to ensure a very predictable behavior of real-time embedded applications and makes them easier to design, implement, test and certify. The underlying principle of this paradigm is to invoke and perform activities and data transfers at fixed time instants [22], [25]. Under this hypothesis, the application state can be accurately determined at any time instant: it is exactly known when the application interacts with a physical environment. Besides determinism, the time-triggered control of system temporal evolution enables also software portability and more efficient programming.

div.head: Time-triggered languages
div.p: Timing models of real-time applications proposed in timetriggered languages permit to assign different activities to the particular time instants. Within these models, each computational task is characterized by its Logical Execution Time (LET) [18]. The task reads its inputs at the beginning of its LET, then it executes within this interval and, exactly at the end of its LET, it makes the results of its computation available to the other tasks that need them. The observable temporal behavior of a task is somehow independent from its physical execution: the time spent from reading program input to writing program output is always the same and is determined by the LET of the task whatever is its actual scheduling or its execution trace. It may induce some delays between the instant when the results are physically ready and the instant when these results are made available but, in turn, it permits to preserve the conformity with the logical model of the application.

Examples of time-triggered languages are the Giotto programming language [12], [13], [15] and the Timing Definition Language [8], [9], [31] which extends Giotto with a compositional model of application. The Extended Timing Definition Language (E-TDL) [19], [20], [21] introduces to the former languages a more flexible and reactive task model.

div.head: Toolchain for time-triggered systems
div.p: This paper presents a work that is part of a tool set and an execution environment aiming to facilitate the development of predictable time-triggered real-time embedded applications. Within this framework, applications are specified through two separate descriptions: their timing definition (expressed in E-TDL) and the purely functional code of tasks (expressed in any programming language, C for example). The applications are executed on the real-time operating system KBR, developed for this purpose at the ONERA. KBR implements the support for E-TDL language features and controls the execution of time-triggered applications by interpreting a control code that is built-in inside it. This control code supervises the timing of application tasks by triggering, in accordance with their timing definition, the different events relative to the progress of the tasks and to the input reading or output writing. This control code is generated by the E-TDL compiler for a given application and a given platform. The compiler needs to ensure that the LET semantics is preserved and the generated code is actually time safe [14]. To this end, it must guarantee the schedulability of the application tasks on the target platform.

div.head: Contribution
div.p: In the context of time-triggered real-time applications modeled with E-TDL, the contributions of this paper are in:

• defining demand functions and algorithms for their calculation tailored to time-triggered systems that may run in multiple modes; • implementing an exact schedulability test under Earliest Deadline First (EDF) [23] for E-TDL systems on a single processor and discussing its complexity; • showing, through simulation, what are the dimensions of the systems whose schedulability can be verified in a reasonable amount of time.

div.head: Organization of the paper
div.p: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the main abstractions of E-TDL and their semantics. In section III, we define the demand functions for E-TDL that allow to quantify the processing time required by the tasks. The schedulability test for E-TDL detailed in Section IV is founded on the processor demand criterion [5], [7] and uses the E-TDL demand functions. Section V includes experimental results based on randomly generated E-TDL systems. They permit to characterize the global functioning and performance of the schedulability test. In Section VI, we discuss related works. Finally, Section VII concludes with a summary of the main contributions and a discussion of future work.

div.head: II. THE E-TDL MODEL
div.p: We hereby recall the elementary model of E-TDL system composed of multiple modules, each running tasks that are grouped into different operational modes. This model is rooted in the Logical Execution Time paradigm [18].

The basic entity in the E-TDL framework is the periodic task τ i = (Φ i , C i , LET i , T i ) characterized by its offset Φ i , its worst case execution time C i , its logical execution time LET i and its period T i . According to the E-TDL semantics, the j-th instance of task τ i is invoked at time instant r i,j such that:
div.formula: ri,j = Φi + (j -1) Ti < j Ti (1)
div.p: and is logically terminated at time instant d i,j such that:
div.formula: di,j = Φi + (j -1) Ti + LETi ≤ j Ti. (2
div.p: Note that in the traditional real-time periodic task model, release and deadline of the j-th instance are not constrained to occur within the time interval [(j -1)T i , jT i ]. In the context of the schedulability analysis, the Logical Execution Time can be used interchangeably with the notion of relative deadline.

Several concurrent tasks may be grouped into a periodic mode that is invoked when the system or its environment is in some specific state that should be handled by this particular mode. Mode m executes periodically, within its mode period T [m], a finite task set τ [m]. For ease of the further analysis we suppose that task sets of different modes do not intersect. The The state of the system and its environment can be described in E-TDL by a certain number of variables (e.g. temperature, speed). A particular change in some of these variables can reflect a significant evolution of the system (e.g. the temperature variable which exceeds a target threshold would indicate that the temperature is climbing past a danger line). When this change is detected, the current operating mode m stops and a new mode m starts in order to handle this particular change in the system. The transition between modes is referred to as mode switch and the condition to operate a mode switch is expressed through some boolean expression. This boolean expression is periodically evaluated in the current mode. The period of this evaluation is the mode switch period T sw (m, m ) and must be declared in the E-TDL description of mode m as a multiple of its hyperperiod H[m]. When evaluated, if the mode switch condition is satisfied, the new mode m is entered. Otherwise, the current mode m continues.

Since the j-th instance of task τ i executes within the interval [r i,j , d i,j ] ∈ [(j -1)T i , jT i ] (see Expressions (1) and ( 2)), there is no active task in τ [m] at mode times that are multiples of the mode hyperperiod
div.formula: H[m], ∀τ i ∈ τ [m] : H[m] mod T i = 0.
div.p: Therefore, tasks of two subsequent modes never overlap and do not access shared variables or actuators concurrently leading to an undefined behavior. In our future work, we plan to allow more flexible mode switch mechanism by refining the behavior of particular tasks during transitional phase [28]. To this end, a new analysis and a support for this feature in operating system should be provided (none of the existing frameworks for time-triggered languages supports it).
The set of all the modes that can be entered as a result of a mode switch declared in mode m at mode time δ is denoted by starting modes(m, δ).

The compositional unit of an E-TDL system is the module. The system executes concurrently the modules from the finite set M odules by sharing processing resources among them. Each module M ∈ M odules can run in one mode at a time. The set of modes in which the module M can run is defined by the finite set Modes[M ]. The mode executed initially by the module M at system start is
div.formula: Init[M ] ∈ Modes[M ].
div.p: The temporal evolution of each module is independent from the evolution of other modules and there is neither hierarchical nor dependency relations between them (e.g. mode switches can occur independently among modules).

A module state is described by a pair (m, δ) where δ is the current mode time in the mode m that the module is executing at a given time instant. The module states of all the concurrently executing modules in the system that may be observed at a given time instant are denoted as parallel configuration ζ of this system. A parallel configuration ζ = ((m 1 , δ 1 ), . . . , (m k , δ k )) is a k-tuple where k = |M odules| is the total number of modules in the system and (m i , δ i ) is the state of the module M i ∈ M odules.
The following example illustrates the concepts introduced above and will serve as a running example in this paper.

div.head: III. PROCESSOR DEMAND CALCULATION
div.p: We first define the demand functions that quantify the maximal amount of processing time required by an E-TDL module. Then we show how these functions can be computed. They will be applied in the next section to establish EDF schedulability test for E-TDL.

div.head: A. Demand functions for E-TDL
div.p: The following definitions are derived from the demand function [5], [7] and permit to quantify the maximum execution time requirement of an E-TDL module over any time interval Δ. During this interval, an E-TDL module can change its operational modes at predefined time instants or stay in the same mode. Therefore, the modeling of processor demand has to account for such possible changes.

The processor demand of a task τ i is the amount of processing time required by τ i that must be entirely executed within a given time interval. With respect to E-TDL module, the computational requirement of its tasks during the continuous execution of the same mode can be evaluated in like manner as for a complete task system that is not subject to mode changes [5].

Various execution patterns that the module can carry out during interval Δ have to be investigated by exploring all potential mode switches. Among all these execution patterns the one that demands the maximum of computation time must be found.
Let Δ H be the length of the time interval between δ and the subsequent time of the hyperperiod:

div.head: IV. EDF SCHEDULABILITY FOR E-TDL
div.p: In this section we provide a test for verifying the schedulability of an E-TDL system running under EDF on a single processor. The test is obtained by combining an exact method with a computationally less complex approximate method. These methods are based on the schedulability conditions presented in the following subsection.

div.head: A. Schedulability conditions for E-TDL
div.p: The schedulability of a task set under EDF on a single processor can be guaranteed if the cumulative demand of computation of the tasks in any interval is never larger than the length of this interval [5]. Within the E-TDL framework, the schedulability analysis is additionally complicated by the mode switches that can occur strictly periodically in the concurrently executing modules.

The approaches that address event-triggered systems [10], [27], [32], when applied to time-triggered systems, can provide only a sufficient schedulability condition (approximate) [19]. By taking into account all timing relations between concurrent activities, an approach, well-suited for time-triggered systems and in particular for those that are modeled with E-TDL, has been proposed [21]. It provides a necessary and sufficient schedulability condition (exact). Both approaches are based on the processor demand criterion [5], [7] and are hereby recalled.
Theorem 1 (Approximate [19], [21]). Let be an E-TDL system defined by a set of modules M odules such that:
div.formula: M ∈M odules max m∈M odes[M ] {U (m)} ≤ 1 (8)
div.p: If for every time interval Δ > 0 :
div.formula: M ∈M odules mdbfM (Δ) ≤ Δ (9)
div.p: then the E-TDL system is schedulable under EDF on a single processor.

The above condition is sufficient because it considers that the largest demands of length Δ in all modules can occur simultaneously what is not necessarily the case of each E-TDL system. This hypothesis may lead to overly pessimism. The overestimation can be eliminated by summing only these demands, from each concurrent module, that may be associated with the same, actually existing, parallel configuration.
Theorem 2 (Exact [21]). Let be an E-TDL system defined by a set of modules M odules such that:
div.formula: M ∈M odules max m∈M odes[M ] {U (m)} ≤ 1(10)
div.p: If for every observable parallel configuration ζ and every time interval Δ > 0:
div.formula: M ∈M odules maxdfM (m, δ, Δ) ≤ Δ(11)
div.p: where (m, δ) is the state of module M in the observable parallel configuration ζ, then the E-TDL system is schedulable under EDF on a single processor.
The exact condition is based on an exhaustive analysis of all the parallel configurations that can be observed when running the system.

div.head: B. Time complexity analysis
div.p: In what follows, we analyze the worst case time complexity of the problem of verifying the schedulability of an E-TDL system with Theorem 1 and then with Theorem 2.

Suppose that, for a given interval Δ, all the values of maxdf M (m, δ, Δ) for all M ∈ M odules and for all their respective module states (m, δ) are known.

div.head: C. Schedulability Test
div.p: Based on the previously described conditions, we propose a schedulability test for E-TDL systems under EDF. The main idea of the test is to apply Theorem 1 for each interval within a feasibility bound and, if it fails, to resort to Theorem 2. In this way, the test can benefit from the efficiency brought by Theorem 1 and from the accuracy enabled by Theorem 2.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In what follows we characterize through various benchmarks the maximal dimensions of the E-TDL systems whose schedulability can be evaluated efficiently with the test proposed above. We compare also the exact method and the approximate method in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. The simulation experiments are carried out on randomly generated E-TDL systems (sets of modules).

div.head: A. Random generation of E-TDL modules
div.p: We propose a method for the random generation of E-TDL systems (their timing specifications).

An E-TDL system, which is represented by a set of E-TDL modules, can be characterized by: a) the number of modules, b) its cumulative maximal processor utilization factor (Equations ( 8) and ( 10)), c) the total number of tasks in all modules.

Given these three parameters, we generate a random set of E-TDL modules. The generation involves two stages. First, since a module is composed of a number of modes, a set of mode candidates is randomly generated. It consists of multiple modes with different numbers of tasks and with different utilization factors. Then, a number of modes is randomly selected from this set of modes and distributed among different modules.

div.head: E-TDL Mode generation policy
div.p: The task set of an E-TDL mode can be described by the number of tasks it contains and their utilization factor (Equation ( 4)). The task set for a mode with a given number of tasks, from 1 to 12, and with a given processor utilization factor, from 0.05 to 0.90, is randomly generated as follows:

• Task periods T i are randomly selected from a set of some predefined integers from 2 to 150. The least common multiple of the selected periods (mode hyperperiod) should not be greater than 150 (this constraint is used to limit the run-time of the test, see Formulas ( 13), ( 14) and ( 15)). • Task processor utilization factors U i are generated using the UUniFast [6] algorithm. For each task τ i , its worst case execution time C i is obtained by multiplying its utilization factor by its period T i (generated as described in the previous point):
div.formula: C i = U i • T i .
div.p: Due to the rounding error effects (worst case execution time must be integer) the task set generation might be repeated a number of times until the final task set utilization is obtained with an absolute precision of 0.05. • The number of tasks with LET i different than the period T i is generated according to a normal distribution with mean equal to the 25% of total number of tasks in the mode and with standard deviation equal to 1. Among these tasks, those that have their offsets Φ i greater than zero are selected according to a normal distribution with mean 20% of their total number and with standard deviation of 1. Then, the values of LET i and offset Φ i are chosen randomly among all admissible numbers using an uniform distribution.

The set of random modes used in all our experiments contains 817 different modes generated according to the rules explained above for each number of tasks from 1 to 12 and each mode utilization factor from 0.05 to 0.90 with a 0.01 step.

div.head: E-TDL System generation policy
div.p: As already mentioned, a set of modules is generated given a number of modules, a cumulative maximal processor utilization factor of these modules and a total number of tasks in the modules.

We first look for a set of modes that is later distributed among the different modules. This set is obtained by randomly adding new modes from the random set (generated as explained above) until the imposed constraints are satisfied. The selected modes are randomly distributed among the modules taking into account that the cumulative maximal processor utilization factor cannot be more than 0.05 of the given value (absolute precision). All mode periods are equal to their hyperperiods. The mode with the highest processor utilization factor within each module is designated as its initial mode. At the end of its period, the mode switches to the other modes are declared. There are no other mode switches.
The procedure of E-TDL system generation was called for every single experiment presented below. All the experiments were run on a 4-core Intel Xeon W3530 2.8 GHz.

div.head: B. Performance evaluation of the test
div.p: A reasonable metric to evaluate the performance of the proposed test is to measure the time of its execution as a function of overall number of tasks in the systems. User without knowledge in the domain of scheduling would intuitively give the dimensions of a system by the number of implemented tasks.

In the following experiments, we measure the time it takes to execute the schedulability test proposed in Section IV on the randomly generated E-TDL systems as a function of their total number of tasks.

Impact of the utilization: In this experiment, we vary the total number of tasks within the system for three ranges of its utilization factor (defined as in Expressions ( 8) and ( 10)). Results of this experiment are illustrated in Figure 6. Each point is the average of time needed to execute the schedulability test. For a given number of tasks and the imposed utilization factor, 4400 randomly generated E-TDL systems were tested (30% with 2, 50% with 3 and 20% with 4 modules).
Since the feasibility bound (Equation ( 15)) increases as the total utilization increases, it takes more time to perform the schedulability analysis for the heavily loaded systems.

Impact of the number of modules: In this experiment, we vary the total number of tasks for the systems composed of different number of modules. Figure 7 shows the average of time needed to execute the schedulability test for the systems having 1, 2, 3 or 4 modules. The experiment covers about 7000 randomly generated E-TDL system (30% with utilization factor 0.6, 50% with 0.7 and 20% with 0.8) for a given number of tasks and the selected number of modules.

We observe that, for a given number of modules, the runtime is, to the certain number of tasks, lower than in the case with less modules (except for the single module system). Beyond this number of tasks, it increases significantly. Indeed, it can be expected that the values of Formula ( 14) are smaller, to a certain point, than the values produced for a case of a smaller number of modules if the factors in their nominators are the same. The run-time of the systems of 3 modules converges to the run-time of the systems of 2 modules but the crossing point is beyond the figure axis range.

div.head: C. Comparison between the exact and the approximate method
div.p: As the test is based on two methods, approximate and exact, we investigate the performance and accuracy of each of them. For this purpose, we lock the test to use either the approximate method (Theorem 1) or the exact method (Theorem 2) for all the intervals within a feasibility bound.

div.head: Performance of the exact and the approximate method:
div.p: In this experiment, we compare the time needed to evaluate the schedulability of the randomly generated E-TDL systems using only the approximate method or only the exact method. The results of the experiment are shown in Figure 8. Each point represents the average execution time of the corresponding schedulability test as a function of task number in the randomly generated E-TDL system. For a given number of tasks, more than 2850 E-TDL systems of 2 modules with utilization factor 0.6 were randomly generated.

The curves of the exact and the approximate methods can be interpreted respectively as an upper bound and a lower bound for the execution time of the test presented in Subsection IV-C which is in fact a combination of these both methods (for that particular experiment setup, the performance of the implemented test is close to the performance of the approximate method). Note that the run-times are with regard to the analytical results obtained in Section IV-B. The runtime of the approximate method should not increase more than linearly (Formula ( 13)). The run-time of the exact method, for the case of 2 modules, can be in the worst case quadratic (Formula ( 14)).

Schedulability ratios for the exact method and for the approximate method: This experiment explores what percentages of the randomly generated systems are proven to be schedulable (schedulability ratio) by the exact method and the approximate method. The experiment covers nearly 480000 randomly generated E-TDL systems (48% with three modules, 52% with four modules) having from 8 to 100 tasks. The results are shown in Figure 9.

The probability for the intervals from distinct modules that their sum exceeds the computational capacity grows together with the utilization factor. In this case, the approximate method fails while the exact one checks if the intervals actually overlay.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Several task models for real-time systems are, to some extent, similar to the E-TDL module. The recurring branching task [2], [3] permits modeling of some restricted forms of the conditional execution. In like manner, the E-TDL module checks mode switch conditions and executes the different modes sequences which, on the contrary, are not necessarily recurrent nor characterized by the same inter-arrival time. In the generalized multiframe non-cyclic model [24] the order of frames is not predetermined and therefore the behavior is neither necessarily cyclic. However, in E-TDL not all modes may be reached from every mode switch. model of E-TDL module is the digraph real-time task [30].

The sequence of the releases of subsequent jobs is described by a directed graph which can also be used to represent the execution and the transitions of modes inside the E-TDL module. The principal difference is that digraph task is based on the sporadic model while E-TDL task and E-TDL mode switch are always periodic.

The parallel between digraph task and E-TDL is also apparent in the iterative approach for calculating maximal demand. This approach was used as well to characterize the number of events occurrence, specified by a finite state machine, within a given interval [33]. All these methods are founded on a characterization of the minimum cycle mean in a digraph [16].

Many schedulability tests [26], [29] for EDF are based on the concept of a busy period [7], [11]. Its implementation for E-TDL would require computing the requirement of the tasks alongside their processor demand (for the system from Example 1 the analysis based on a busy period would stop at the length of the interval 10 while the feasibility bound that is in use equals 60).

Compositional schedulability analysis of the modular systems can be performed by Real Time Calculus [32]. It computes the total highest demand of the system as a sum of the highest demands in the particular modules. In E-TDL this approach can be considered only as a sufficient condition (Theorem 1). More precise way of compositional analysis for time-triggered system is thus proposed (Theorem 2).

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: In this paper, we implemented an exact schedulability test under EDF on a single processor for time-triggered systems that are modeled within the E-TDL framework. This test bridges the gap between model driven engineering of timetriggered systems and scheduling theory.

Our evaluations in Section V show that the test can verify schedulability for the systems of limited size. For several successfully implemented with the time-triggered languages systems [13], [17] (no more than dozen tasks in total, 2-4 tasks in each mode), the capacity of our test would be grossly under-exploited.

Several approximations of the demand function [1] and the method for identifying its recurrent term [34], [35] can be used to reduce the time needed for calculation of maximal processor demand. Also, the pseudo-polynomial test for asynchronous periodic task sets [26] can be applied. Further improvement can be made by increasing the step of our test.

The similarities between E-TDL module and generalized multiframe task, outlined in previous section, can be explored to compute more efficiently the processor demand generated during execution of a sequence of modes. In particular, the method proposed for non cyclic GMF [4] can provide an upper bound for processor demand of such sequences of modes.

Besides improving performance of the test, our ongoing work is towards a more flexible mode switch mechanism that lifts the constraint of hyperperiod without jeopardizing the well timedness rule of any task [20].

The parallel configurations ζ 1 , . . . , ζ n (n is the total number of configurations) are obtained by a procedure fully explained in[21]. It exploits the relations between task offsets, task periods and mode periods of the concurrently executing modules. Without going further into details, we describe roughly its main concepts. First, it finds the potential time instants of mode starts. Example 5. Let m 1 and m 2 be two modes of the same module such that m 1 is an initial mode, T sw (m 1 , m 2 ) = 9, T [m 2 ] = 6 and there are no other mode switches. As the number of evaluations of mode switch from m 1 to m 2 , k 1 , and the number of periods of m 2 that have elapsed, k 2 , are supposed to be unlimited, m 2 can start at any time instant t start (m 2 ) = 9 • k 1 + 6 • k 2 which must be consequently a multiple of gcd(9, 6) = 3.Then, knowing factors of potential start time instants of every mode, it finds, for a set of modes from distinct modules, all their mode times that satisfy the Chinese remainder theorem and so can be observed concurrently.
